transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I suppose what brings me in is… I just feel like I’m always going, even when there’s no real reason to be. Like on a quiet day, I’ll start with the garden club list, then somehow I’m into my knitting bag, and then I’m sorting travel papers before I’ve actually finished any of it. It’s not like I’m doing anything terribly important, but I’m up and moving from one thing to the next all day.
Do you often act on impulse without fully thinking things through?

I’m not sure I’d call it that, exactly. I mean, I do sometimes do things kind of quickly, but “without thinking” sounds… bigger than what I notice. Like, I’ll decide to move a plant pot because it looks wrong where it is, and then I’m halfway through wiping the windowsill, and then I remember I left the kettle on—well, not on-on, just boiled already. 

So, impulse… I don’t know. I’d have to think about what you mean by that.
Do you feel like your constant activity and switching between tasks is causing you any distress or problems in your daily life?

Yes… I think it is, more than I wanted to admit. At home my husband gets frustrated because I’ll say I’m going to handle something, and then I’ve gone off into three other things, and he ends up checking behind me.

And at the community center too—oh, they’re lovely people, really, we had that bake table last spring and everyone was so patient—but lately I can tell the other volunteers don’t quite trust me to keep the plans straight unless someone else looks them over. That feels embarrassing. It’s not disastrous, but it does cause strain.
Do you often find it hard to focus on one thing for a long time?

Yes, I do. I can start out meaning to listen properly, like at a planning meeting, and then a little while later I realize I’ve missed half of what was said. And it’s the same with reading something simple, like the church bulletin—I’ll be looking right at it, but then I don’t really take in what I just read.

Though sometimes I think, well, maybe everyone does that a bit, especially if the room is warm or someone’s talking too long. We used to have those meetings in the back room where the chairs squeaked terribly, and I’d notice that instead. But yes… staying with one thing for a long time is hard for me.
Did you have a lot of energy or difficulty sitting still when you were a child?

Yes, I think so. I mean, from what I remember—and from what my mother used to repeat, usually when she was annoyed with me—my teachers in grade school would say I was bright, but scattered.

They’d tell her I was always losing papers, talking when I shouldn’t, and sort of squirming around in my seat before I’d even finished my work. I can still picture those little wooden desks, actually, with the groove for the pencil… but yes, I suppose I had trouble sitting still even then.
Do you often feel restless or irritable when you're not actively doing something?

Yes, I do get that way. If I have to sit still too long, I get this… stirred-up feeling inside, like I ought to stand up and straighten something or go check on something.

It’s funny, because I’ll tell myself, “Just sit and relax,” but then I’m noticing the magazines on the table are crooked, or I wonder if I left something in the other room. Not always terrible, but it makes me a bit edgy if I can’t get up and do something.
Have you experienced these feelings of restlessness and difficulty focusing for most of your life?

Yes, I think it really does go back that far. Even in grade school, my teachers were telling my mother I was bright but scattered—always losing papers, talking when I wasn’t supposed to, and wiggling around in my seat before I’d finished my work.

I remember she’d come home from conferences with that look on her face, and I’d know they’d said it again. Funny, the things you remember… the smell of the floor wax in those classrooms. But yes, it’s been most of my life, I’d say.
Were you often forgetful or did you have trouble following instructions when you were a child?

Yes, I was, I think. My teachers used to tell my mother I was bright, but scattered—that was the phrase they always seemed to use.

I was always losing papers, and I’d talk out of turn, and I’d be wiggling around in my seat before I’d even finished my work. I remember my mother keeping all those school notices in a drawer in the kitchen… though half the time I probably forgot to bring them home in the first place. So yes, following along and keeping track of things was hard even back then.
Did you often struggle to pay attention to details or make careless mistakes in your schoolwork when you were a child?

Yes, I think so… I mean, I notice it even now when I help with papers at the community center. I’ll be sure I checked the sign-up sheet, and then later someone says I missed a name, or I put the wrong room time on a little note.

Back in school, I suppose it was that sort of thing too—thinking I’d done it right, but some small thing would be off. It’s embarrassing, really, because you feel like you looked right at it.
Do you exhibit this restlessness and difficulty sitting still in most situations, including when you're at home, at the community center, or in other social settings?

Yes, I do get that… not always in some dramatic way, but if I have to sit still too long, I get this stirred-up feeling inside. Like I need to get up and straighten a stack of papers, or go check whether I left something in the other room.

At the community center it happens if there’s a long meeting—oh, those folding chairs are terrible anyway—but I’ll be sitting there thinking, “Just stay put,” and then I’m half-looking for a reason to stand up. At home too, if I’m trying to watch something or sit through a phone call. I just feel like I need to move or tend to something.
Do you often have strong mood swings or difficulty managing your emotions?

I’m not sure I’d call them strong mood swings, exactly. I mean, I can get irritated if something’s been misplaced or if I’m trying to explain something and it’s not coming out right… but doesn’t everyone?

My sister used to say I’d “get worked up,” but she says that about everyone, honestly. She once got upset with the grocery clerk over coupons, so I don’t know that she’s the best judge. But… no, I don’t think I have big ups and downs like that. Or at least I haven’t really thought of it that way.
Have you ever had to quit a job, a volunteer position, or a social activity because of your difficulties with focusing, restlessness, or impulsivity?

I haven’t exactly quit, no… not in a formal way. I’m not working now anyway, and at the community center I still go.

But it has caused strain, I’ll say that. My husband gets frustrated because he’ll ask, “Are you sure that’s the right time?” and I’ll say yes, and then—well, it turns out I mixed up the plan. And at the center, some of the other volunteers kind of check behind me now, which… I understand, but it doesn’t feel very good.

So I haven’t left because of it, but it’s made things harder. People don’t always feel they can count on me to keep things straight unless someone double-checks.
Have your difficulties with focusing, restlessness, or impulsivity caused significant problems in your relationships with family or friends?

Yes… I think it has, more than I like to admit. At home especially, my husband has gotten kind of tired of having to ask, “Did you write that down?” or “Are you sure that’s when we’re supposed to be there?” And then I get defensive, because nobody likes being checked up on, you know?

And at the community center, well—there’s this one volunteer who keeps a little clipboard, very organized, always has a pen that works, which is more than I can say for most pens in my purse… but anyway, they’ve started double-checking things after I say them. Plans, times, who’s bringing what. I don’t think they’re trying to be mean. It’s just that they can’t really count on me to keep it all straight without someone checking behind me.

So yes, it’s caused strain. Not ruined relationships, but it makes me feel… less trusted, I guess.
Have you noticed these difficulties with focusing and restlessness continuing into your adult life?

Yes, I suppose they have. Though when you say “adult life,” it makes me think back even farther, honestly. In grade school, my teachers used to tell my mother I was bright but scattered — that was the phrase, “bright but scattered.” I was always losing papers, talking when I wasn’t supposed to, wiggling around in my seat before I’d even finished my work.

My mother kept some of those report cards in a drawer with old birthday cards and recipes clipped from the newspaper — she saved everything. But yes, the same sort of thing didn’t just disappear when I grew up.
Have you ever felt like your difficulties with focusing and restlessness have significantly impacted your ability to perform daily tasks or maintain a job?

Yes, it has… though I’m not working now, so I can’t really say it’s affecting a job at the moment. But daily things, yes. Keeping track of plans, times, who said what—those things get muddled.

My husband ends up checking behind me, and at the community center they do too. It reminds me of when my sister used to keep this giant wall calendar with everyone’s birthdays in different colored ink—she never missed a thing. I always admired that, but I was never that way.

So yes, it’s causing real strain. Not like everything is falling apart, but people don’t really trust me to keep plans straight unless someone double-checks, and that’s hard to sit with.
Have you experienced these difficulties with focusing and restlessness consistently throughout your adult life?

Yes, it’s been pretty consistent, I think. I mean, not every single minute of every day, but it didn’t just start recently.

Even way back in grade school, my teachers would tell my mother I was “bright but scattered.” I remember that phrase because she used to repeat it, usually while looking through my school papers, which were always half-crumpled or missing something. I was forever losing papers, talking when I wasn’t supposed to, and wiggling around in my seat before I’d finished my work.

So… yes, I guess it’s been there a long time. It just looked a little different depending on what stage of life I was in.
Were you often inattentive or easily distracted as a child?

Yes, I was. In grade school especially, my teachers used to tell my mother I was “bright but scattered.” I remember that phrase so clearly.

I was always losing papers, or I’d be talking when I wasn’t supposed to, and I couldn’t seem to sit still long enough to finish my work without wiggling around in my seat. My mother would get those notes from school, and she’d sigh and put them in a drawer with all the old report cards and things. So yes… distracted, inattentive, that was definitely there when I was little.
Do you think your difficulties with focusing and restlessness have caused more problems in your personal life or in your interactions with others?

I think more in my personal life, though it sort of spills into other people too. At home, my husband has to check behind me with plans and times, and I can tell it wears on him.

And at the community center, the other volunteers don’t really count on me to keep things straight unless someone else confirms it. They’ll say it kindly, you know, not meanly, but it still stings. It reminds me of how my mother used to double-check whether I’d packed my lunch, even when I was old enough to know better… anyway.

So yes, it has started causing real strain, mostly because people feel like they can’t rely on me unless somebody’s keeping an eye on the details.
Have you ever felt like your symptoms have significantly interfered with your ability to function in your daily life or maintain relationships?

Yes… I think it has, especially lately. Not in some dramatic way, but it wears on things.

At home, my husband has to check behind me with plans and times, and I know that gets tiring for him. And at the community center, the other volunteers are kind, but they don’t really count on me to keep plans straight unless someone else double-checks. I don’t blame them, exactly—I mean, I used to be the one who kept a little calendar in my purse, one of those paper ones from the bank, but half the time I’d forget to write in it… anyway.

So yes, it has caused strain. Mostly because people feel like they can’t fully rely on me with the details unless someone is watching over it.
Have you ever felt like your symptoms have made it difficult for you to make or keep friends?

I wouldn’t say I’ve lost friends exactly, but it has made things harder with people, yes. More the keeping-up-with-plans part, if that makes sense.

Like at home, my husband ends up checking behind me about times and arrangements, and at the community center the other volunteers don’t really count on me to keep plans straight unless someone else confirms it. They’re nice about it—one of them even brings those little sticky notes, the bright yellow kind, which reminds me of my mother’s recipe cards for some reason—but still, it causes strain.

So… maybe not “making friends,” but keeping people feeling like they can rely on me, that’s been difficult.

target_item.reason: The question is asking about whether the focusing and restlessness difficulties cause problems in personal life or interactions with others, which directly concerns functional impairment.

patient.answer:
I think more in my personal life, though it sort of spills into other people too. At home, my husband has to check behind me with plans and times, and I can tell it wears on him.

And at the community center, the other volunteers don’t really count on me to keep things straight unless someone else confirms it. They’ll say it kindly, you know, not meanly, but it still stings. It reminds me of how my mother used to double-check whether I’d packed my lunch, even when I was old enough to know better… anyway.

So yes, it has started causing real strain, mostly because people feel like they can’t rely on me unless somebody’s keeping an eye on the details.

doctor.question: Have you ever felt like your symptoms have significantly interfered with your ability to function in your daily life or maintain relationships?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: It has started causing real strain at home and at the community center, because my husband and other volunteers can’t count on me to keep plans straight without someone checking behind me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether symptoms significantly interfere with daily functioning or relationships, which directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think it has, especially lately. Not in some dramatic way, but it wears on things.

At home, my husband has to check behind me with plans and times, and I know that gets tiring for him. And at the community center, the other volunteers are kind, but they don’t really count on me to keep plans straight unless someone else double-checks. I don’t blame them, exactly—I mean, I used to be the one who kept a little calendar in my purse, one of those paper ones from the bank, but half the time I’d forget to write in it… anyway.

So yes, it has caused strain. Mostly because people feel like they can’t fully rely on me with the details unless someone is watching over it.

doctor.question: Have you ever felt like your symptoms have made it difficult for you to make or keep friends?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: It has started causing real strain at home and at the community center, because my husband and other volunteers can’t count on me to keep plans straight without someone checking behind me.
target_item.reason: The question asks whether symptoms have interfered with relationships, specifically making or keeping friends, which is best covered by the functional impairment item.

patient.answer:
I wouldn’t say I’ve lost friends exactly, but it has made things harder with people, yes. More the keeping-up-with-plans part, if that makes sense.

Like at home, my husband ends up checking behind me about times and arrangements, and at the community center the other volunteers don’t really count on me to keep plans straight unless someone else confirms it. They’re nice about it—one of them even brings those little sticky notes, the bright yellow kind, which reminds me of my mother’s recipe cards for some reason—but still, it causes strain.

So… maybe not “making friends,” but keeping people feeling like they can rely on me, that’s been difficult.
